subtopic: PROVISION FOR SEPARATION OF AIR LINES FROM RAILWAY OWNERSHIP

speechtext:
Mr. STANLEY KNOWLES (Winnipeg North Centre) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 21, to amend the Aeronautics Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to reword section 14 of the Aeronautics Act so as to give effect to the intent of parliament at the time the section was enacted. This is the section that was supposed to provide for the separation of air lines from ownership by railway companies within one year after V-E day. The section as it stands says that this is to take place within one year after the termination of the war in Europe as fixed by order in council. The delay in proclaiming the end of the war has made the effective date of this section an indefinitely movable feast. This bill settles the matter by inserting a definite date for section 14 to come into effect, namely, December 31, 1947.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

subtopic: UKRAINIANS IN SALZBURG CAMP, AUSTRIA

speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Secretary of State for External Affairs): Mr. Speaker, I should like to supplement the information I gave the house on Wednesday in answering a question of the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) about displaced persons in Salzburg camp, Austria.
The government has communicated with the director general of UNRRA who has supplied the following information concerning this matter: No information is available at UNRRA headquarters, Washington, to identify the 3,500 Ukrainians in question. UNRRA, Washington, have therefore undertaken to cable this complaint to their headquarters in London, where they should be able to get the further necessary details.

The following is the additional information I wished to give. The Salzburg area is under the control of the United States military authorities, who have the final responsibility for the screening of all displaced persons. It is the United States military who have the entire responsibility for screening collaborators. UNRRA screening is done only to determine the eligibility of the individual for entry into the camp under the terms of the UNRRA resolutions. Officials of the Soviet Union are not members of either of these screening groups.
This information, I think, will be of interest to those who were so much disturbed about the matter, because they were under the impression that these screening groups were controlled by Soviet officials.

There has been delay in the issuing of the application form. subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
Last evening the minister gave a statement, in response to our repeated inquiries, rvhich in some measure covered the policy of his department since he took over. To the extent that he dealt with the consolidation and reorganization he has in view I believe the statement cleared up many questions in the minds of hon. members on this side of the house, but he did not go on to give us that statement of policy and purpose in regard to our forces for which we have asked him and his predecessor ever since peace broke out-and for that expression I am indebted to the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario.
In his speech last evening the minister mentioned that there was a great deal of idle speculation and imagination in many of the questions asked from this side of the house. I do not believe that is correct, but if there were any speculation or imagination it was forced upon us because of the fact that the minister had not made the statement he so obviously should have made. The thing comes down to this. Great changes have been made in the administration of this department and in its policies since the minister took office. I want to say right now that I would have thought changes of this nature would have called for an expression of policy, perhaps along the lines of the white papers which are so often issued in Great Britain, one of which was issued in connection with defence at the end of the war. The minister also said that he thought his statement last evening was premature, because the matter could have been discussed on the estimates, and he still seems to have in his mind the idea that members of the house are not entitled to the information for which they are asking. It is not a matter of being premature. The first opportunity should have been taken by the minister to make a statement, not on estimates but on policy. This was the first opportunity. The only statement he has made about the future set-up of the forces, and the policy he is following, apart from the departmental organization, is that had he recruited up to 100 per cent of his predecessor's irreducible minimum it would have been difficult later to make a change. I find great difficulty in understanding that statement, unless it means that the only change the minister was contemplating was a reduction in the force that he might have recruited, had he gone up to 100 per cent. I do not believe there is anyone in Canada who believes that the figure set last year was one which should have been open to any reduction whatever, in any one of the services.

Militia Act

It seemed to me, too, that as far as he did explain the decision not to recruit up to strength, he placed it only on the ground of economy. He did not give us any other grounds as to why 75 per cent of the establishment was satisfactory. How long does the minister expect that the country will not be able to afford more than 75 per cent of that minimum?
If there has been any concern, either in the forces or in the country, it has been because we live in the future. In everything we do, the question whether we have confidence in what our government is doing, or in what we are doing ourselves, depends upon how far we can see into the future, and whether we can see that what we are doing now is leading us to a condition of security and progress. That applies to the army, just as much as to anything else.
I ask the minister the direct question, whether this twenty-five per cent cut or, as he wishes to describe it, the decision not to recruit up to strength, is based solely on economy. Did the minister make the decision himself, with the consent of the government, or did he ask the advice of the defence council before he decided not to recruit up to strength?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: I fully appreciate what the minister has just said, but at the same time if his statement, as to his power to amend establishments is correct, though it may sound rather silly to stand here today and even consider the reduction of all establishments simultaneously, nevertheless as I see it that is a possibility. I think we might as well face these facts. In introducing the bill I believe the minister said a few changes were being made to make it more flexible, and so on, but I regard it as

Militia Act
an insidious bill, because it places in one man the power to disband the Canadian army, according to the minister's own statement.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
Possibly the minister might explain the necessity for the change at all. In the past the governor in council has been able to operate under the Militia Act and make the necessary regulations. Certainly the number of regulations that have been made would not indicate very much holding back by reason of the fact that power rested with the governor in council. For what reason do these various sections now provide that the minister may make regulations? I looked up section 139 of the act, and it indicates power to make regulations. It says:
The governor in council may make regulations for carrying this act into effect, for the organization, discipline, efficiency and good government generally of the militia, and for anything requiring to be done in connection with the military defence of Canada.
That is what the section is at the present time. But it is to have an addition whereby the governor in council may empower the minister to make regulations for the purposes mentioned in subsection 1 of this section. In other words, all the governor in council has to do is to pass a general order in council granting the minister powers so wide that they permit him to do everything he considers necessary' for efficiency, organization, discipline and good government, and anything in connection with the military defence of Canada. That makes the minister an absolute dictator in respect of the defence of this country, once he secures an order from, the governor in council granting him the right to make regulations. Why does the minister now ask that the Militia Act be changed so that henceforth he may make the necessary regulations, instead of as heretofore, I believe for about eighty years, having that right remain in the governor in council? What is the reason for it? What is behind it? What are the purposes?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
The purpose of the bill is to enable the administration of the armed forces to be carried on in a direct and efficient manner. I am informed that during the war there were thousands of submissions to the governor in council making minor changes in establishments. That required a good deal of paper work, and much time, of the governor in council and of everyone concerned. Most of these were minor changes, such as changing the establishment of an infantry battalion from one having, let us say, three carpenters to one having only two carpenters, and that kind of thing. The submissions came down to detail as fine as that, and most of the changes
were of that kind. In order to make the operation simpler this provision was drafted in its present form. It will be noticed that the definition of "prescribed" in the Militia Act was this:
(j)	"prescribed" means prescribed by this act or by regulations made hereunder.
And then "regulations" was defined in this way:
(k)	"regulations" means regulations made by the governor in council under the authority of this act.
We ran into a number of instances in which powers to do certain things were prescribed, and frequently they were minor, unimportant and technical. In those instances it was felt that the governor in council might delegate authority to the minister.
I should tell the hon. member that this is a usual provision in legislation in force in other countries, and also that it is modeled on the Xaval Service Act, which was passed by parliament in 1944.
The main characteristics and size of the armed forces are dealt with under an entirely different provision. Here we are dealing with units. But the main characteristics are dealt with under section 5 of the bill, which would explain section 14 of the act, and states-
The organization of the Canadian army shall be as from time to time prescribed by the governor in council.	,
And that power rests with the governor in council.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
Apparently the
answer for this departure from the provisions of the Militia Act, which has been in effect for more than eighty years, is that it is in the interests of efficiency, and arises also out of the multiplicity of regulations which have to be certified by the governor in council. The purpose of this bill is

Militia Act
to that fact. The hon. member for Vancouver South is an old parliamentarian and he must know the rules. The answer I think is indicated by the Prime Minister's remarks that there is close cooperation.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION

speechtext:
I do not want the minister or the committee to think I am flogging a dead horse, but I refer again to section 1, paragraph (j) which gives certain powers to the minister. I fully appreciate-and I have reason to be able to appreciate it-the desirability of having flexibility in connection with a great many "regulations", and having those regulations brought to finality by the minister. I am quite aware of what the minister pointed out as to the powers under section 8 of the bill, which amends subsection 2, paragraph (a) of section 20 of the act to read:
The Canadian army shall consist of such units . . .
And so forth, and also section 32 which reads as follows:
Section one hundred and thirty-nine of the said act is amended by adding thereto the following subsection:
"(2) Except where the power to prescribe or make regulations is by other sections of this act reserved exclusively to the governor in council, the governor in council may empower the minister to make regulations for the purposes mentioned in subsection one of this section."
Taken in the extreme-and I repeat it, it is the extreme case-the minister has power to disband the Canadian army. It is all very well for the minister to say that that is exaggerated and that no minister who ever did such a thing could live, but I again point out to him that I am not talking about today or even tomorrow. If this house writes into the act section 1, paragraph (j) it is possible that there could come a time when, under some other form of government, perhaps, if you wish, different from what we have at the moment, if one can conceive of such a government coming into power, it would be possible to disband the Canadian army without regard to parliament or even to the governor in council. There has been altogether too much said about "it cannot happen here." Some of us are realists enough to appreciate the fact
Militia Act

that strange things can happen. Therefore, if there were to remain in the Militia Act that which gave the minister power to take such an extreme act as I have suggested, namely that of disbanding the Canadian army,
I think we are justified in our stand in trying to prevent such difficulties which might conceivably arise. I am in no way desiring to obstruct the giving of power to the minister to create efficiency within the Canadian army, to set up that type of machinery which will permit the normal flow of regulations to pass over his desk and become effective in the army. But I do think that if at the same time we give the minister virtually unlimited power in regard to reduction by means of the discontinuance of an establishment and carrying that to the limit, ultimately disbanding the Canadian army, we are writing into the act that which the minister himself does not want written into it. The point remains, and I strongly suggest to the minister that there be some qualification in regard to regulations which does not appear in section 32 and section 22. It should definitely appear there, qualifying those regulations by which the minister and the minister alone has the final power. I do not think it takes away one iota from the purpose of the bill, and it does protect the Canadian people from the extreme action which would be possible were this particular subsection to be permitted to remain in its present form. Will the minister be good enough to tell the committee what he thinks of that point?

These sections do purport to confer powers; but section 2, paragraph (j), confers no powers whatever. It defines regulations as being in two groups, one that can be made by the governor in council and the other by the minister. It is purely a defining section.
With regard to the extreme case, the hon. member suggests that under one of these other provisions such as section 8, amending section 20, the minister can disband the Canadian army. I must submit that that is not so at all. What he could do would be to change individual units, as has happened, but this section certainly would not give him any such power as was suggested.

This afternoon, while I was reading the bill now before the house, the amendment I want to introduce occurred to me.
Under section 9 of the Militia Act, "Professors in colleges and universities, and teachers in religious orders" are exempt from liability to service. I submit to my hon. friends- and you will admit that the matter is worth considering-the case of teachers in the primary, secondary and normal schools of our province. It so happens that during the last war, three lay teachers on the staff of a primary school in Saint Philippe d'Argenteuil were called up in one month. As a result, needless to say, school schedules were upset and one school even had to be closed. In addition to the listed categories, would it not be advisable to exempt for the duration of their current contract which, according to the school code, runs for one year, except where special agreements are in effect, teachers employed by the Department of Education.
Should an emergency develop in February or March, necessitating the calling up of teachers in our primary schools-and everyone knows that- they are more numerous than our secondary schools-what would happen if they were called up all at the same time? In all fairness, and without prejudice, I believe that we must take into consideration the plight of our school boards, normal schools and secondary schools in such an emergency.	By
secondary schools, I mean "high schools", because at home, in Lachute, half of the high school staff is made up of male lay teachers who would therefore be called up. I wish, therefore, with the leave of this honourable house to submit the following amendment: "That section 4 be amended by adding the words "and teachers of secondary and primary schools, duly accepted by the appropriate provincial department of education, for the duration of the current school year" after the words "religious orders" at the end af line 45, page 2.
I do not ask for a permanent exemption, but I feel that our school boards should not run the risk of losing a teacher during the school term. Such an amendment would not be unfair since, under our school legislation, teachers are hired for one year only. In order to avoid placing the school boards in an embarrassing situation and possibly depriving children of their education, it would only be fair to grant such teachers an exemption until the end of the school term, that is until June of each year; this would give the school boards four months, that is May, June, July and August, to hire female teachers.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
This is one of those sections to which some of us referred yesterday when we said that the bill was giving too great power to both the minister and the governor in council. The result of this would be to create not an army of parliament but an army of the government. This particular section provides that the governor in council shall have certain powers, while other sections provide that the minister shall have certain powers.
I suggest that under this section the control of the army, in fact the whole organization of the army, is being taken out of the hands of parliament and placed in the hands of the governor in council. It is obvious on reading the section that that is the case. Parliament might make provision for organization and administration of the army along certain lines, but under this section- the governor in council could pass contradictory regulations and orders in council and undo the will of parliament. The section immediately following this one brings the point I have in mind out in the open because by that section parliament will surrender to the governor in council the power to say what shall be the term of service during peace.
According to the explanatory notes, the parliament of Canada under the old act laid down just how the army should be organized and I do not see why that power should not be reserved to parliament. Why should we hand over to the governor in. council the right to make all regulations as to organization?

We should draw a distinction between what is proper-administration by order in council- and what is improper-legislation by order in council. I submit that the power to organize the army given here confers the power to legislate. The power to administer is an entirely different matter. The governor in council must have that power.
I think there is contained in section 5 a principle which we should not sanction and I ask the minister to explain why he has not used the words "administration of the Canadian army" rather than "organization of the Canadian army". I think "organization" is the wrong word to use here because it gives the governor in council the power to legislate and undo what parliament has done.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: I have the greatest respect for parliament, but I doubt if parliament would like to be entrusted with the work of organizing the Canadian army. I do not think that is a proper function of parliament.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: What does the minister mean by "organization"?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: That means the major establishment of corps, divisions, commands and brigades and setting the main characteristics of the army. It refers also to their relations to each other.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
I do not altogether agree and I direct the attention of the minister to the explanatory note. The old section laid down the principles by which the army should be organized and the minister did n-ot have the power to depart from those principles. He had the power to make detailed regulations as to the administration of the army on the basis of the legislation passed by parliament. I submit it is a dangerous principle to allow the organization to rest in the hands of the minister.
We have said in effect that the army shall consist of an active force and a reserve force. That is organization. If we give to the governor in council the power to organize, the governor in council can say that the army shall not consist of an active and a reserve force but shall be all active or all reserve. That is what organization means. I most certainly think the word "organization" should be changed to "administration". I should like to hear some better explanation from the minister before I change my mind. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, that the word "organization" where it appears in the proposed new section 14 be deleted and the word "administration" substituted therefor.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: The reason for the proposed new section 14 is, as I stated before, that it was felt desirable that the major organization, the characteristic corps, brigades, number of divisions and all major matters of that kind, should be dealt with by the governor in council as a matter of major policy and not be dealt with as a matter of administration by either the minister, if it comes within his power, or by the various military commanders if it comes within their scope. It was because this was regarded as a matter of major importance that it was put into this form, so that the power of dealing with the organization of the Canadian army shall rest with the governor in council, rather than within the power of the minister or of a military commander. I hope, in view of that explanation, my learned friends will not press their amendment because the word "administration" means something quite different.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
I realize that, and that is why I moved the amendment. Administration is so different from organization that I did not feel it was proper to give what I regard as purely a legislative function to the governor in council. I think the proper place for the provision which the minister has in mind would be under section 7 which proposes a new section 19 of the act, where power is given to the governor in council to lay down commands and headquarters of commands and to change them from time to time. If the power which the minister is now seeking were
limited in that way and put in as a new section 19 or perhaps 19A there would be no objection, if the power were specifically restricted to the power to make changes within formations. But merely to use the word "organization," is giving far too wide a power because, as I pointed out, under section 9, which creates a new section 22, parliament itself lays down what shall be the organization of the Canadian army. I do not think the minister will quarrel with that interpretation. I suggest that there is no use in parliament laying down what shall be the organization if the minister reserves to the governor in council the power to change that organization. If the minister will restrict the sphere within which the governor in council may have power to organize I will withdraw my amendment.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: The suggestion that the new section 22 confers upon parliament any right to determine the organization of the army surely cannot be seriously pressed for a second by the hon. member. All that that section does is to provide that there shall be a ceiling on the active force. It says that the active force shall not consist of more than so many men, and we are going to amend that so that the number will actually be stated there. But that has nothing to do with organization. It just imposes a ceiling. I hope I have not correctly understood the hon. member to suggest that parliament is the place where the active force should be organized. I submit with some confidence to this house that parliament does not want to be charged with the task of organizing the army. It is not the place to do it. What is involved here is a description of the corps, how many divisions and that kind of technical thing, which parliament, I am sure, would not like to see itself take up its time with. In view of this explanation I hope that the hon. member will not press his amendment.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION

That was my point. It gives to the governor in council the power to make regulations within that specific sphere. I wish to say a few words about section 5. I realize that, when in committee of the whole, we have to limit our remarks to the section being considered; however, as the scope of this section has an extremely wide scope, I believe it will permit me to discuss with sufficient thoroughness the question I would like to submit to the house. The objects of section 5 are twofold: first, fully to entrust the organization of the Canadian army to the governor in council; second, to remove section 14 from the Act. What was the purport of section 14 of the Militia Act which is to disappear? It was worded as follows:
14. The militia of Canada shall be divided into active and reserve militia.
2.	The active militia shall consist of,
(a) corps raised by voluntary enlistment;
(b) corps raised by ballot.
3.	The reserve militia shall be raised and maintained under regulations prescribed by the governor in council.
To remove section 14, is, for all practical purposes, to abolish the distinction between the active army and the reserve army. The upshot will be that Canada will have a single army, the Canadian army as defined in paragraph b of section 2, which is as follows:
"Canadian army" means all the military forces of Canada other than the Royal Canadian Navy and the Royal Canadian Air Force and the reserves thereof.
And to show that we are really doing away with the reserve army, it will be noted that on several occasions the word "reserve" was deleted. As to the army, the Royal Air Force or Royal Navy, they all remain, but in connection with the army, the reserve does not enter into the picture. May be called upon to serve in the militia, according to section 8 of the act which reads as follows: All the male inhabitants of Canada, of the age of eighteen years and upwards, and under sixty, not exempt
It is clear, Mr. Chairman, that if there are in Canada three million men between 18 and 60 years, they will not all be called under arms at the same time. However, they are all liable to be called, and as soon as they are called, by lot or otherwise, they form part of the active army, and become subject to the requirements of the present active army as they were to those of the active militia which are being done away with.
In granting the governor general power to organize as he sees fit the Canadian army, and by reason of the fact that we abolish at the same time, to all intents and purposes, the distinction between active army and reserve army, he is given the power to enrol or call under arms, in peace time as well as war time, all the men of Canada between the ages of 18 and 60.
To those who claim that my interpretation is wrong I say read again paragraph (b) of section 2 and you will see that I am right.

Perhaps there is some
confusion in the mind of the hon. member. What was commonly known to us as the reserve army and officially designated as non-permanent active militia was never mentioned in the Militia Act. The reserve army was part of the active militia. Under section 139 of the Militia Act which authorized the governor in council to draw up all necessary regulations dealing with "the organization, discipline or good administration" of the army.
The king's regulations and orders were drawn up and applied to all non-permanent forces, and the active militia was divided into permanent and non-permanent forces. They existed under section 1 of the king's regulations and orders and not under the Militia Act, especially not under section 14. That which my hon. friend finds in the old section 14 is called "the reserve militia", which is not the same thing as the non-permanent force. What used to be the non-permanent force is now the reserve army. The governor in council was authorized to call up and organize that force, known as reserve militia, but never did so. When the Canadian army as it now exists was renamed it was designated as the active army and the reserve army under section 139 which was and is still in force. The said section is still in force and authorized the governor in council to control, administer, and organize the army. In fact, section 1 of the king's regulations and orders has simply been amended or changed. As regards the permanent force and the non-

permanent force the section states that the Canadian army consists of the active force, a field force, a brigade group, as was mentioned last year, and the reserve force. It corresponds exactly, under a new name, to the non-permanent active militia which existed before the war. The reserve force is in no way abolished, as my hon. friend believes. It will continue as before.
There is another point that I would like to stress. My hon. friend claims that under section 5, in repealing section 14 and replacing it by the new provision set out in the bill we are authorizing the governor in council to pass drastic measures after the manner of Hitler. I would point out to him that there is no connection whatever between former section 14 and the new provision. Former section 14 is repealed. It had become obsolete and impractical. The new section has been introduced- in order to facilitate an efficient reorganization of our militia. The new section bears the same number as the provision which is being repealed, but this is purely coincidental. It is not supposed to serve the same purpose as former section 14.

I am afraid that the hon. member for St. Maurice-Lafleche (Mr. Hamel) is under some misapprehension with regard to the purpose of the bill. In my estimation it is a bill of which we should be proud as its chief purpose is to replace the words "Canadian army" by the words "Canadian militia". The term militia just as aptly applies to an army or any organized unit within a non-sovereign state. In the United States, for instance, it applies to the forces of the various states, because they are not sovereign. The American army is that. . . .

Militia Act

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: The states are sovereign.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION

. . . which is established by the federal government in Washington. I feel therefore that discarding the term Canadian militia in favour of Canadian army removes the suggestion of colonialism.
As for the concern voiced by the hon. member for St. Maurice-Lafleche over section 47, it must be remembered that the new section 47 simply states that:
The governor in council may order the Canadian army or any units thereof to drill or train for such period in each year as he may prescribe.
Which means that at a given period of the year the governor in council may prescribe that a certain artillery reserve or active force regiment must go into training at Petawawa from such a date to such a date. That is what it means. Training, not active service. That is all it means, nothing more. Now as to the last fear expressed by the hon. member, I am convinced that he cannot help thinking that conscription could be imposed in time of peace. I respectfully submit that if he would read this bill, together with the king's regulations and orders in so far as they apply to the Canadian army, he will see that in order to join the Canadian army, one must enlist voluntarily. Thus, if my friend still has any doubts in this respect, I see no objection why these words would not appear in section 9 of the bill, amending section 22 of the act. I can see no objection to adding here the words "and men voluntarily enrolled," in the English version, and the words "du nombre d'ofiiciers et d'hommes enroles volontairement", in the French text. In my opinion, that would dispel any misgivings or doubts which my hon. friend may have and which,-happily for him, -are mere fancy.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: Would the minister tell us why it was found necessary to reserve the period of service in the army to be determined by the governor in council, instead of carrying on the practice, which apparently has existed ever since the Militia Act came into existence, of having it fixed in the act?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
It is fixed in the act by section 15 in the following words:
The period of service in time of peace shall be,
(a)	for the active militia, three years;
(b)	for the reserve militia, such period as is prescribed.
It will be noticedi that power is given the governor in council to fix the period of service for the reserve militia, and the only period specifically fixed in section 15 is the three-year period for the active militia. Consideration is being given to the desirability of taking on a certain proportion of the active force for a longer period than three years. It is well known that most members of the permanent force actually serve for more than three years; and if they are willing voluntarily to offer themselves for a period longer than three years it would seem to be in their interest as well as in the interests of the country that they should be enlisted for a longer period and given the security which comes from having a longer period of enlistment, while from the point of view of the service there would be greater certainty of continuity. For that reason this change, which applies only to the active force, all of which must be enlisted voluntarily, is suggested as being useful.

I know this has happened in the past; and some time when the estimates for the Department of National Defence are being considered, I propose to ask the minister how many men have been taken into the interim force in the last eighteen months, and have been let out for various reasons. I suggest to the minister that there should be a definite time limit. Is a man to be enlisted in the services today, and be able to get out in six months; or can he get out in a year or two years? Is -it his will that governs, once he gets in? What kind of army will you have if you have not set down, 100 per cent, a definite term of service?
Money is to be spent on it, and I say, if you are to have a five-year term of service, then let us know it is to be five years. If it is to be
Militia Act

a two-year term of service, let us know it is to be two years, and let us insert in the act what the term of service will be for a man serving in the forces.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: As the hon. member surely ought to know, this has nothing whatever to do with the interim force.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: Why has it not?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: Why should it have? Here wre are dealing with the active and the reserve armies, not with the interim force.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
You are dealing with
the active army?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: I suggest that the minister is trying to have regulations dealing with the active army, and that there is to be no definite term of service. Therefore there is insecurity for the man, insecurity for the service and insecurity for the public who are paying the money. Consequently I say that in this act there should be a definite term of service.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: The hon. member has brought up something about the interim force. The arrangement with regard to the interim force was that it wouild terminate on September 30, 1947, and that arrangement is being carried out. But this provision, as the hon member must know, on reading it, has nothing whatever to do with the interim force.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the minister is putting words into my mouth. The point is this-

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: Oh, Oh.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
Oh, all right; you fellows don't like it, so you can make all the noise you like. I don't need to take a lesson from you fellows over there about this, anyway.
We are setting up a force; and because I used the expression "interim force" the minister has turned my words around. He knows I am talking about the men who are to be permanently stationed in the army, men who will make the army their livelihood. I want to know what term of service will be set up for those men-not today or tomorrow.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: At the present time the term of service for which men have voluntarily signed on in the active army is three years.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
Then why not insert
it in the act?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: Because it is proposed to enlist some men for five years. That gives them more security.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
Then I suggest that
if it is proposed to take some men for five years there should be a proviso in the act stating that certain men will be in for five years.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: And how many of them? How will that be provided in an act of parliament?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: That is your business- to find out how to do it. It is not mine.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: We like this way of doing it.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: I understood the minister to say that this section applies only to members of the permanent force.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: No, I did not say that.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: I am sorry; I understood that.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: No.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: If that is not so, or if it applies to both the reserve and the permanent forces, may I ask the term of service so far as the reserve army is concerned, if one has been set.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: Three years.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
In other words, the
three years which prevailed before will continue?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: In that event I suggest that should be put into the act, and made definite, so that civilians, who are in a rather different position from permanent soldiers, may know definitely, when they sign their attestation papers, they have signed on for the normal period of three years, unless under a later provision they may get out on six months' notice.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
It is in the attestation
papers that they sign. As I said before, this proposed change does not make any change with regard to the reserve army, because the period of service in the reserve army previously was fixed by the governor in council. That is left just as it is.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
It was fixed at three
years.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
I should like to ask a
question in respect of those who may sign up for three or five years, as the case may be. Let us suppose that a young man who seeks to make the army his life's work signs up for one of those periods. Has he any assurance

Militia Act
that at the end of that time he will be permitted to sign up again, provided that he is healthy and fit?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
There is no assurance;
provided that a man is physically fit and is willing to continue his service, the ordinary rule is that he is carried on.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: Do I understand from the minister, then, that we shall have men in the army who have two different terms of service, some for three years and some for five years?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: Yes; that is right.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: Is that contemplated?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: Will that not make for confusion?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: Not at all.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: What about the man who wishes to join the army, but who wants to know whether he is joining for three years or five years?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: He will know when he signs up.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
What about the civilian who is contemplating joining the army, and wants to know whether he will fall into the five-year or the three-year category? It seems to us that it is a dangerous precedent to permit the governor in council to have the power in time of peace to change the period of service in the armed forces. It also seems to us that they should be able to make up their minds in advance as to the best length of time for a man to serve, so that all people who are considering this type of career will know exactly where they stand.
What are the reasons which are influencing the minister or his advisers in coming to the decision that a five-year term is desirable, and why have they not yet been able to make up their minds, so that it might be written into the act?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: As I said before, the reason is that it is considered desirable that we should be in a position to offer to a man the term of service that seems appropriate, in the interests of the service, at the time when the offer is made. At the present time it is three years because that is the limit fixed in the act for both active army and reserve army. It is being considered that five years would be a more desirable term but that has not been definitely decided.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: Is it thought by the army authorities that they will find it easier to enlist men if there is this flexibility as to the term of service?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: I think the primary consideration is the interest of the service, although there is undoubtedly combined with it the interest of the man. He will have a greater feeling of security and more confidence in its being a career. In that way undoubtedly it would assist in recruiting.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: There is a principle at stake here, the control of parliament over the active forces. As I understand the law, at the present time enlistment in what is known as the active militia must be for three years. That means that parliament has direct control over the period of service in the active militia. If the difficulty is that the department is not quite sure whether it will want this type of soldier for five years and that type for only three, why not put in a provision that the term of service shall be for a maximum of five years? That would retain the control of parliament over the maximum period of service and it would give the department some scope. It is a serious thing to take away that control from parliament and it has been changes of this kind that have caused most of the trouble in getting this bill through the house. I see no reason why parliament should be deprived of this particular control.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: In what way would it be desirable that the period be fixed as a maximum? I do not see the advantage of that.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: The way the new bill is worded you would be able to enlist a man for seven years, for ten years or for fifteen years. That may or may not be desirable. I do not think this change should be made without the approval of parliament. If you had a maximum of five years you would not be taking the control away from parliament.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: I cannot see what the advantage would be.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: Will the minister allow the section to stand and give this matter further consideration?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: I must say that I do not see any advantage in the suggestion, and I must say equally that I do not see any objection, except that it might give the impression to the men that they could not be reengaged for more than five years.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
That would not be so because, as the act now reads, there is a three-year limitation and the man knows he can reenlist. The difficulty here is that you are taking the
Militia Act

control away from parliament. We are in peace time and parliament should control these matters wherever possible. I realize that in some cases there must be some control by the department or preferably by the governor in council, but here you are taking away from parliament control which you do not have to take away. I suggest that the minister allow this particular section to stand and give it further consideration.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: I do not see how the control of parliament would affect this situation, either for or against. It seems to me that this is not a question of great principle or moment. It is not as though we were imposing restrictions on the term of service in the army as was done with the German army after world war I when it was limited to a long-term army. There is no such question involved here and it seems to me that the service requirements are the ones which should prevail. I do mot see any real purpose to be gained by imposing a limitation. If the hon. member really presses it I shall certainly give the matter consideration and discuss it with the officers.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
There is another factor to be considered. Under the amendment the governor in council could authorize enlistment for only one or two years. In that case the country would be losing because we have an investment in these men. They are trained and they are more valuable soldiers at the end of three or four years than at the end of one year.
Too wide powers are being given to the governor in council in this case. I suggest that, in so far as the men on full-time duty in the active force are concerned, parliament should set the time. It could be either three years or five years; there could be two alternate periods, but it is not right just to say that the governor in council may decide that a man can enlist for six months or six years or ten years. It is going too far. I ask the minister in all earnestness to give further consideration to this particular question.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: I shall be glad to.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
At the time of enlistment in the Canadian army I take it that a man signs some form of contract with the government of Canada or the Department ol National Defence, wherein he and the government know there is a term of service of three or five years, as the case may be. Both parties to the contract are fully aware of that condition at the time of signature. Am I to understand from section 17 that the man would be

permitted to break that contract, except in the case of an emergency such as a war, by giving six months' notice to his commanding officer?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: Let us look at the matter from the other angle. Under what conditions may the government dispense with the services of that man before the three or five-year period is up? Is there a tacit obligation on the government to continue to retain that man in the service if he wishes to remain until the end of his first period of engagement or until a time when his services in a military way no longer would be required? May we have a brief statement on that phase of that question?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: A man may withdraw from any unit of the Canadian army on giving notice in accordance with both the old and the proposed section 17. However, in. accordance with the king's regulations and orders for the Canadian army he must, in addition, pay a sum of money related to the months of service which he has still to serve on his period of enlistment as set out in his attestation.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: That is a condition of his attestation?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: He has to buy himself out.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: Yes. Then, as regards the separation of a man from the army at the request of the crown, that, can be done at any time. A man can be discharged.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: Is the general principle this, that if there is an adverse report on the soldier his commanding officer may recommend his dismissal? What about completing his term of service?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: There is a regulation providing for discharge for various reasons.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
A pertinent point has been raised by the hon. member for Regina City. It has worked a great hardship on many oi the men who had enlisted in the now active force or in the permanent forces of the crown, and it is being applied in a particularly vicious manner at the present time when there is a large number of permanent force noncommissioned officers and men who have served for a long number of years in the old permanent force, men who served with distinction during this war, some of them receiving promotion to the rank of commissioned officers, and they are now being told that their services are no longer required. They are being let out when they are within sight

of the goal for which they have been striving namely, to get a pension as a result of twenty years of service. There are men today who have given fifteen, sixteen, eighteen and nineteen years of service in the permanent force and who are now being compulsorily discharged and are not being allowed to complete only six months more of service in some cases in order to entitle them to a permanent force pension, which they have served all these years in the hope of obtaining. They are not being discharged because they are inefficient, for they have the highest recommendations from the officers under whom they have-served. They are being discharged solely for the reason that His Majesty has no further use for their services. These are not satisfactory conditions. When a man who joins the permanent force is asked to sign a contract-t-hat he will serve for three years and has to pay a certain sum of money if he breaks that contract, I think a similar obligation rests on the government if the government breaks its contract with that man.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: May I ask my hon. friend this question? He knows about buying out of the service.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: I bought out of the government service myself. I know all about it.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: My hon. friend knows about it perhaps better than I do. He knows that the principle of buying out of the service exists in Great Britain to this day. My hon. friend must know that in the last war the policy which has been set in motion by this government was set in motion by the British government.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: That does not make it right.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: That is not the point.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: I was in the British navy myself and I know something about buying out. I think I know something about pensions too, and something about the industrial life of this country, and when an industry contracts-

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Chairman; are we not discussing a particular bill?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
I am quite familiar with the circumstances of buying out of the government service because, when I volunteered to go over in world war I, it was necessary for me to purchase my discharge from another government service. Therefore I am familiar with the conditions. All I am saying is that if the government imposes those conditions on a man, a similar obligation rests upon the government.
Militia Act

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: I want to direct a few questions to the minister. What is the meaning of "Canadian army" as referred to in section 15? How is the army to be recruited? Is it to be on a voluntary basis only or not? If this bill is enacted, will the governor in council-I ask for a yes or no answer-have power to call for service for a certain period the male citizens of Canada from eighteen to sixty years of age, or any of them?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
The Canadian army is defined by paragraph (b) of section 2 as it will be amended if this bill passes. "Canadian army" means:
. . . all the military forces of Canada other than the Royal Canadian Navy and the Royal Canadian Air Force and the reserves thereof.
It means in fact the active army and the reserve army. The active army consists of those full-time soldiers who have voluntarily enlisted for the period of their service, and the reserve army means those part-time soldiers who voluntarily enlisted for the period of their service. Both are voluntary enlistments and either may withdraw at the end of six months in peace time.
In reply to my hon. friend's final question, there is no change made in the existing position by this bill.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: That is not the answer I expected. My question was this. If this bill is enacted, will the governor in council have power-yes or no; only a very short answer is required-to call for service for a certain period the male citizens of Canada from eighteen to sixty years of age, or any of them? The only answer can be yes or no.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: If there is a levee en masse as provided for in section 8 of the act, which has been in effect since 1868, and has never been used, that may be done.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: The answer is yes.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: I have not yet heard the minister's answer to the point raised by the hon. member for Nanaimo. I do not think there is much use in our suggesting improvements in the section if no attention is paid to suggestions that are made. If there is this grievance on the part of the men 'as pointed out by the hon. member for Nanaimo, and if it can be removed, let us remove it.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
I thought the hon. member for Nanaimo was making a speech and not asking a question, but if it was a question and if an answer is required I would say that I am informed that the only reasons for which men have been released from the active army-are age, medical unfitness or inefficiency. If
>44
Militia Act

there are any who have been released for any other reasons that are not covered by the regulations, then I would be very glad to have the hon. member or anyone else call these cases to my attention, because I am assured that there are not any. There is a considerable number of men in the active army who continued their service throughout the war and who now wish to be retired, or who have reached the age or the condition of medical fitness when they need to be retired. If there are any who have been improperly retired, then I should be glad to look into the cases and see that any necessary action is taken.
I should add that persons who have over ten years permanent service are now pensionable under part V of the Militia Pension Act as it was changed last year.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: I shall be pleased to supply the minister with at least one name of a warrant officer in the old permanent force who is being discharged not because he is inefficient, not because he is medically unfit and not because he has reached the age of retirement.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: I shall be glad to hear of that single case and will look into it.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: There is a section under which we operated during the war-and I might say that the government took great advantage of it-under which, if an officer or a man had no job, he was put out, and the minister is well aware of that. Are there not many officers and men being put out of the army today under that section?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: None.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: I refer to the phrase "no suitable employment"; I think I am right. I wish the minister would answer my question.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: I said "none", I should think sufficiently audibly for the hon. member to hear if he was listening.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: Will the minister say that the army is different in that respect from the air force or the navy? Is the army unique in this extraordinary position? Some of us know perfectly well that there were men in the R.C.A.F. whose services were no longer required'-period. That had nothing to do with the physical fitness, nothing to do with inefficiency, nothing to do with age; their services were no longer required.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
Of course that happened in the air force in which, as everyone knows, there was a great surplus of flying personnel at

one stage of the war. The provisions with regard to discharge in the navy, army and air force are quite different.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, if I am still in order and I trust I am, in regard to the R.C.A.E., at the conclusion of hostilities and shortly subsequent to V-J day, in the complete absence of any policy in regard to the force that was to be formed as a permanent force there were hundreds of worth-while and worthy young men whose great ambition it was to make the R.C.A.F. their career, who, as a result of the absence of policy as laid down by this government, went out on civvy street and are still there. There was no force at that time other than the war force, whether the same thing has happened in the army or not. Good men have been lost to the army as a result of that. I should like the minister to comment in that regard.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: I wish to take an objection to the remarks of the hon. member that there was no policy in the air force. The policy was announced immediately after the war. The permanent force was set up on a definite basis, and the men who were kept in the permanent force were kept on the basis of the establishment which had been set up.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: I do not wish to get into a debate with the former minister of national defence for air; nor do I wish to use information which I have as a result of active service. I simply should like to say to him that, as a result of being a commanding officer of a release centre in those days, I cannot subscribe to his statement.

speechtext: Shall the section carry?

speechtext: The minister undertook to allow this section to stand.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: I ask that the amendment to paragraph 15 be allowed to stand.

speechtext: I wish to ask a question on paragraph 18. It refers to two kinds of soldiers, first, those' who have voluntarily enlisted and, second, those who have been called upon to serve in the Canadian army. First, what is meant by those who have been called upon to serve?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: Carried.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
This is not going to carry quite so quickly as the minister seems to think. Last evening I asked the Minister of National Defence a question. I wish to know under what authority military district 13 has been abolished. He was very kind to me. He read this section of the bill as printed, and I am going to read it back to him because he may be one of those people who learn better by hearing than by looking. I want his opinion after I have finished. The section reads:
19. The governor in council may,
(a)	direct that any portion of Canada shall
be a military district for the purposes of this act, and may alter the limits of any such district;	_
(b)	cause two or more districts to be grouped together for the purposes of command and administration; and
(c)	divide any military districts into subdistricts, brigade, regimental and company divisions, as appears expedient.
Then, in the explanatory note underneath, we find the following;
It is proposed to abolish the present division of Canada into military districts and to organize the country into military commands which may be divided into areas. The proposed amendment reflects this change.
I point out, sir, that the bill which we have before us states that the government proposes to do something which has already been done and completely done. Before he answers, may I repeat the gratuitous advice I gave him last night, that there is no authority for the changes which have already been made. We can now disagree again but I want to affirm the opinion I expressed at that time.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
The authority is in the section of the Militia Act just read by the hon. member, which is section 19. I will read it again:
The governor in council may,
(a)	direct that any portion of Canada shall be a military district for the purposes of this Act, and may alter the limits of any such district;
(b)	cause two or more districts to be grouped together for the purposes of command and administration; and
(c)	divide any military districts into subdistricts, brigade, regimental and company divisions, as appears expedient.
On January 11, 1946, the governor in council approved an order setting up the reallocation of military districts, grouping them together for the purposes of command and administration under five commands. One of them included the western command, British Columbia, Alberta, northwest territories, the Yhikon -military districts Nos. 11 and 13 and northwest territories and Yukon. That was pursuant to the statute. It gave effect to it, and it was in accordance with the authority conferred by the statute.

2. Appointments to be made from time to time in pursuance of this order shall be made by the governors general in council.

Then the schedule follows:
1.	Designation.
2.	General description of command.
3.	Definition-area of operational command by military districts.
Then follows a list of the five commands, a general description of the command and a definition of the areas. It seems to me that the minister has been needlessly and uselessly evasive in connection with this matter. We understand and have understood quite well, ever since the order in council which he has read, which came out in January of last year, that there were to be set up and were actually set up in Canada, five commands. But that is an entirely different matter from the abolition of military district No. 13 and its headquarters, which took place only on

Militia Act
December 30 or 31, 1946, or, in other words, about a year after the order in council which he is quoting. That order in council, as I understand it, did not give authority for the abolition of these headquarters. It gave authority for the setting up of five commands, and at the time these commands were set up we were assured that the various military headquarters would continue to function. The abolition of headquarters which has taken place is, I contend, as the hon. member for Calgary West contends, contrary to section 19 of the Militia Act. There was no authority for the abolition of the headquarters, which abolition actually took place at the end of last 3'ear, without the authority of this parliament; and the department and the government are very much out of order in having put through that abolition.
It is of no use for the minister to try to evade the matter by saying that General Worthington is the D.O.C. of military district No. 13 headquarters. That may be a nice fiction to put before us here, who presumably know nothing about it. As a matter of actual fact, however, orders were issued that M.D. No. 13 headquarters would come to an end at the end of December, and henceforth the headquarters at Calgary and the former D.O.C. would be known as the rear headquarters of command, the northwest command. That went into effect, and as far as the reserve units were concerned it was forbidden to address letters to M.D. No. 13 headquarters. It had been washed out; it was finished, and everybody was told so. It is of no use for the minister at the present time to try to maintain an absolutely senseless position and say that the thing still exists. It does not exist; it has been wiped out, and that without authority.
Furthermore, I should like to ask the minister two or three questions on the matter. First, was any investigation made of the costs of placing command headquarters at Edmonton as compared with Calgary before the move was mentioned? If such an investigation of costs were made, what were the findings? As a matter of fact, my information is that no such investigation ever took place but that an investigation was ordered after the move had been announced and after there had been a great deal of complaint. My second question is, what were the findings of the investigation ordered after the move had been made, and what is to be the relative cost to the people of Canada of keeping the entire command headquarters at Calgary as compared with moving it to Edmonton? As I said during the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, my own
investigation and the information I have secured lead me to believe it will impose a heavy additional expense on the department and on Canadian taxpayers, an expense which, in my opinion, is entirely unwarranted unless the minister can produce good reasons to indicate that moving the headquarters is absolutely necessary on strategic or other grounds of that kind, and that thereby much additional expense is warranted, which I do not think he can do.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
The primary reason for
making the change was strategic, as I said yesterday. Anyone examining a map of Canada and considering the developments that have occurred in the west and northwest since the war would realize that those making such a decision on strategic grounds were acting with common sense. I am personally in no position to judge the matter from a purely military point of view, but the slightest examination of a map would indicate that the decision was sensible.
With regard to the economic factors, it is quite obvious that the combining of two military districts located as close together as these were must result in a considerable saving of man-power and other expenses. The other night one hon. member from Calgary said that Edmonton was only three or four hours away if he travelled fast enough, and on that ground it would seem reasonable, if it is strategically desirable, to combine the two and save something in man-power and other costs.

He has said that there would be a saving of $27,000 a year on manpower, and that there would be a certain saving in connection with light and heat. One can well imagine the saving in light and heat when he is told that much the same area will be required. That saving would be 
negligible. I can assure the minister that heating is certainly no cheaper in Edmonton than it is in Calgary. We will say that the saving in light and heat amounts to $5,000 a year-which I doubt very much. That makes a total of $32,000. Immediately one must consider the cost of moving the people concerned, which is a minimum of $140,000. I was told that, before it was over it would probably amount to $200,000.
There is the further cost of over $5,000 a month which will have to be paid in respect of separated family allowances to the families of the men now living in Calgary, who must continue to live there because they cannot possibly get houses in Edmonton. That $5,000 a month will go on for a very considerable length of time. There is the further fact that nearly all the permanent force units are in Calgary and are to remain there. Two-thirds of the reserve force units are in the southern part of the province and a considerable number of staff officers will have to spend the major part of their time in Calgary, away from headquarters. Each one of them will draw $7 a day command pay during the time he is in Calgary, and the transportation expenses of each have to be paid.
I contend that the extra amount of money which will be required for these staff officers alone, travelling to Calgary, over and above the amount of travelling they would have to do if this move were not made will amount in a year to at least two or three times the possible savings the minister has yet been able to mention.
The minister mentions a few figures like that, of savings that are to take place, and expects to convince us that it is an economic matter. As (a matter of fact, on the ground of economy his argument is absolutely ridiculous. If he could put up a good argument on strategic grounds, then I might be prepared to be convinced. As I remember it, when this matter was under discussion one suggestion was that in the case of redesignation, rearrangement and even disbandment, it was not a matter which should ever be referred to the minister. I took the view, as I recall it, that questions of the redesignation of units, the rearrangement or disbandment of them, were matters on which the minister, as the responsible political head of the department, should be consulted and which he should approve. I must confess that personally I felt that was a matter for which the minister as a member of the government could properly take responsibility. As in a good many other things, if he felt it was a question which involved broad considerations he would refer it to his cabinet colleagues for their views, though it might not require a formal order in council to carry the thing through; and that is still my feeling. I still believe that with the thousands of units in the Canadian army it should not be necessary to make a formal submission to council in order to redesignate a unit or even disband one, but that is not something on which I feel strongly at all. It is a question upon which I certainly would place myself, as I am sure the present minister would, completely in the hands of the house. There has been a good deal of talk in this house that we should not have these thousands of orders in council. We are met constantly with the reproach that the government is passing thousands upon thousands of orders in council, and they are held out in the newspapers as an example of dictatorial powers and so on.
It seems to me that this is a matter on which the head of the department could properly decide, as minister, without the formality of an order in council, but that is only my personal opinion. That was the view I held when I was head of the department, but it is not one, I must say, that I hold with any tremendous degree of firmness. If it is felt that this is a matter which should be decided by the cabinet as a whole I cannot see any objection to that. My feeling was that it was a matter which the minister, as head of the department and the man responsible to

parliament, should approve, that it was not a matter which should be decided by the staff or by the officers of the department. I must say I did feel it was a matter which the minister should be able to decide.
